Julius Caesar’s invasion of 55 BC failed. In AD 43 Emperor Claudius conquered almost all of Britain. The Romans stayed for 400 years, until AD 410, and never conquered what is now Scotland.

After the Romans left in AD 410, tribes from northern Europe invaded. By about AD 600 Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were established, mainly in what is now England. Their languages are the basis of modern English.
Vikings from Denmark and Norway first raided in AD 789, then settled in the east of England and Scotland. Alfred the Great defeated them, but many stayed in the Danelaw.
In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings: the last successful foreign invasion of England.
Missionaries from Ireland spread Christianity in the north; St Augustine led missionaries from Rome in the south and became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

The Middle Ages · Life in the UK
Conwy Castle, built by Edward I to hold Wales

The period after the Norman Conquest until about 1485 is the Middle Ages (the medieval period). It was a time of almost constant war, but also when Parliament, the legal system and the English language took shape.

In 1284 Edward I introduced the Statute of Rhuddlan, annexing Wales to the Crown of England. Castles such as Conwy and Caernarvon held it. The last Welsh rebellions were defeated by the middle of the 15th century, and English laws and language were introduced.
In 1314 the Scots, led by Robert the Bruce, defeated the English at the Battle of Bannockburn. Scotland remained unconquered by the English.
Ireland was independent at first. The English came as troops to help the Irish king and stayed. By 1200 they ruled the Pale, an area around Dublin. Some lords elsewhere accepted the English king.

Knights fought in the Crusades for the Holy Land. The Hundred Years War with France actually lasted 116 years. At Agincourt (1415) Henry V’s outnumbered army beat the French. The English left France in the 1450s.

The same system developed in southern Scotland. In the north of Scotland and in Ireland, land was owned by clans (prominent families).
The Normans used feudalism: the king gave land to lords in return for help in war; landowners sent men to the army.

Most peasants were serfs: they farmed a small area of their lord’s land, worked for the lord and could not move away. The same system developed in southern Scotland. In the north of Scotland and Ireland, land was owned by clans (prominent families).
In 1348 the Black Death (probably plague) killed one third of England’s population, and a similar proportion in Scotland and Wales.

Afterwards fewer cereal crops were needed, labour was short and peasants demanded higher wages. New classes appeared: the gentry (owners of large areas of land) and a strong middle class in the towns.
In Ireland the Black Death killed many in the Pale, and English-controlled territory shrank for a time.
Magna Carta: where British rights begin
Its ideas run through to today’s human rights law
King John must accept that even the king is subject to the law
No one can be held prisoner unlawfully; every prisoner has the right to a court hearing
Confirms the rights of Parliament and the limits of the king’s power
Parliament grew out of the king’s council of advisers: important noblemen and Church leaders.

In 1215 King John was forced by his noblemen to agree to the Magna Carta (the Great Charter). It established that even the king was subject to the law, protected the rights of the nobility, and limited the king’s power to collect taxes and make or change laws.

English parliaments were called when the king needed to consult nobles, especially to raise money. Two Houses formed: the House of Lords (nobility, great landowners, bishops) and the House of Commons (knights and wealthy town people, elected by a small part of the population).
Scotland’s Parliament had three Houses, called Estates: the lords, the commons and the clergy.
Judges began to be independent of the government. In England, judges developed common law by precedent and tradition; in Scotland, laws were codified (written down).
Many English words come in pairs with similar meanings, one from each: demand (French) and ask (Anglo-Saxon).
Windsor Castle: built in the Middle Ages and still in use today
By <mark>1400</mark> official documents in England were written in English, and English was the preferred language of the royal court and Parliament.

Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in English: pilgrims travelling to Canterbury tell each other stories. It was one of the first books printed by William Caxton, the first person in England to print books with a printing press.
In Scotland many spoke Gaelic and the Scots language developed. John Barbour wrote The Bruce about Bannockburn.
Castles were built across Britain and Ireland; Windsor and Edinburgh are still in use. Great cathedrals such as Lincoln were built; York Minster is famous for its stained glass.
English wool was a very important export. Skilled people came to work: weavers from France, engineers from Germany, glass makers from Italy, canal builders from Holland.
